locator.text: Display 124.5, p. 124, in the proof of Theorem 1.1

provenance.note: machine audit: worker, gate, reviewer; not confirmed by a human

verdicts.summary: Lean uses a different formula here. No declaration was found in NavierStokes/ stating the identity for a general multi-index α and a general time order m. The Lean's dilation is `rescale a b g = fun z => a • g (z.1, b • z.2)`, and the force f_ν of (10.22) is `scaledVelocity ν f = rescale (√ν) (√ν)⁻¹ f`, i.e. a = ν^{1/2}, b = ν^{-1/2}. On that substitution the three instances the Lean does state match the paper's exponent exactly: |α|=0, m=1 gives factor a = ν^{1/2} = ν^{(1-0)/2}; |α|=1, m=0 gives a·b = 1 = ν^{(1-1)/2}; the Laplacian (the |α|=2 contraction) gives a·b² = ν^{-1/2} = ν^{(1-2)/2}. Higher |α| and higher m are stated nowhere I found. What the paper draws from the general identity in the next sentence — f_ν still smooth and compactly supported — the Lean obtains without any derivative formula, from rescale_smooth and CompactPositiveTimeSupport.spatialScale; and the R3 force class (CandidateProperties.force_smooth, force_support) imposes no decay bounds, so the general-|α| form is not needed for Theorem 1.1 as formalized. The closest exact analogue in the repository, iteratedFDeriv_scale (iteratedFDeriv n (scale ell f) x = (ell*(ell⁻¹)^n) • iteratedFDeriv n f (ell⁻¹ • x)), is in Euler/PhysicalL2Scaling.lean, which is out of scope for this audit and is purely spatial (no ∂_t^m).
